faq.answer: Preferring familiar routine does not prove self-preservation Nine. Accessibility, scarcity, pain, caregiving, sensory regulation, or recovery can require predictability; compare resource conditions and whether chosen priorities resume.
faq.question: Does preferring familiar routine prove self-preservation Nine?

faq.answer: Comfort should be separated from priority avoidance by recording its endpoint and consequence: restorative comfort supports re-entry into a chosen task, while displacement repeatedly consumes the protected time without a deliberate decision.
faq.question: How should comfort be separated from priority avoidance?

faq.answer: A useful matched comparison observes the same routine under adequate resources and genuine scarcity, while holding the task and available time as constant; behavior that follows necessity weakens the subtype interpretation.
faq.question: Which matched comparison is useful for this subtype?

sections.body_md: The hypothesis asks whether familiar activity helps postpone a personally important priority while preserving immediate steadiness. Comfort by itself is ordinary and provides no type evidence.
sections.title: Frame comfort as a secondary observation

sections.body_md: Observe one routine when food, money, time, and rest are adequate, then compare it during real scarcity. A subtype reading should weaken when behavior tracks resource constraints more closely than conflict or priority.
sections.title: Compare the same person across resource conditions

sections.body_md: Self-preservation here names a traditional attention comparison rather than evidence about bodily mechanisms, physiology, or a universal survival system. Material needs remain real regardless of typology.
sections.title: Use attention language, not bodily mechanism claims

sections.body_md: A person may be highly productive in maintenance tasks while still delaying a chosen conversation or direction. Visible busyness neither confirms nor refutes the secondary hypothesis without priority data.
sections.title: Allow visible activity and practical competence

sections.body_md: Shift work, insecure housing, disability, pain, caregiving, sensory regulation, food access, and financial volatility can make routine or comfort protective and necessary rather than avoidant.
sections.title: Account for necessity and accessibility

sections.body_md: Confidence should fall when rest or routine has a clear endpoint, restores capacity, and is followed by the planned difficult task without external pressure or concealed resentment.
sections.title: Look for comfort followed by deliberate re-entry

sections.body_md: Instrument-specific findings cannot establish a universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence. Treat routine, comfort, and priority records as local observations requiring human review.
sections.title: Keep subtype inference modest

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: For five days, choose one comfort routine, one maintenance task, and one personally important action that competes for the same time block.

Observable signal: Record resource sufficiency, physical access needs, chosen priority, routine start and stop, interruption response, and whether the important action resumes.

Page-specific signal: Compare the same comfort pattern on a well-resourced day with a day shaped by scarcity, pain, caregiving, or sleep loss.

Alternative explanation: Check poverty, disability, sensory regulation, recovery, shift work, household duty, food access, and unstable housing before inferring motive.

Reflection prompt: Identify one routine that restored capacity and one that displaced a chosen priority, then revise the secondary hypothesis separately for each.

seo.description: Type Nine self-preservation is a traditional secondary hypothesis linking a core-Nine stability pattern with attention to routine, comfort, familiar activity, maintenance, and material continuity. It does not describe bodily mechanisms. Repetition may instead reflect poverty, disability, chronic workload, caregiving, recovery, sensory needs, or a rational need for predictable access.
seo.title: Type Nine self-preservation: routine comfort as a secondary hypothesis
